issues.item: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: This strategy is socially anxious/interpersonal in content and is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by war-zone danger cues, hypervigilant threat monitoring, and trauma-memory reactivation. The other strategies and threat/memory items coherently reflect trauma-related safety management, but rehearsing conversations before any interaction targets a different problem domain that is not represented elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, or Memory. Given the formulation, maladaptive strategies should plausibly feed back into triggers/threat/memory; this item does not connect well to those active nodes.

vignette: Alec had always been drawn to helping others, which is why he spent two years working as a relief worker in a war-torn region. The memories of that time still lingered vividly in his mind, like the smell of smoke and sweat that clung to him long after he returned home. One particular incident stood out – the sound of children crying in the aftermath of a bombing raid, their small bodies torn apart by shrapnel. Alec's own heart racing as he rushed to help, the image seared into his mind like a branding iron. When kids cried in public nowadays, Alec felt that same heart racing sensation wash over him, transporting him back to that chaotic scene. It was as if the trigger had unlocked a door in his mind, allowing the memories to flood out without warning. The sound became more real than normal life – he could almost feel the dust and debris underfoot, taste the metallic tang of fear on his tongue. In an attempt to regain control, Alec tried to remind himself that it could have been worse; after all, he had made it back home in one piece. This downward comparison was a coping mechanism he'd honed during his time overseas – "at least I'm not still there" became his go-to phrase when anxiety threatened to overwhelm him. However, this strategy only provided temporary relief. The memories continued to haunt him, their vividness and intensity making it difficult for Alec to distinguish them from reality. Sometimes, the emotions would surface without any clear image or memory – just a deep-seated sense of unease that he couldn't shake. In these moments, Alec's mind began to scan his surroundings for signs of threat, as if danger lurked around every corner. He'd constantly check the room, noticing potential weapons or objects that could be used against him. Even when others assured him he was safe, he found it impossible to believe them; in his experience, safety was an illusion. Alec's occupation as a jeweler required attention to detail and focus, but these days he struggled to concentrate. His back had to be against the wall where he could see the room – anything less made him feel like a sitting duck. The sound of children crying still triggered those memories, now intertwined with his hypervigilance for potential threats. When he wasn't working, Alec tried to force himself to think only positive thoughts – if he focused on good things, maybe the bad would fade away. Yet this strategy only seemed to push the darkness further down, where it simmered just below the surface. As time passed, Alec began to notice how his behavior was affecting those around him. His coworkers commented on his constant scanning of the room; friends stopped inviting him out because he'd become too jumpy and irritable. It dawned on him that maybe these coping mechanisms weren't working as well as he thought – perhaps they were even making things worse. What finally brought Alec to seek help was a particularly harrowing flashback, triggered by an unexpected touch from a coworker. For the first time in years, he felt truly lost and alone – scared of what his own mind might do next.
